utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC

utterances.text: I am Anthony Abell good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LIVINGSTON
utterances.text: John Livingston, good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to assure myself that all of the appellants are able to understand the proceedings in a language that they can fully comprehend. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, I am Petar Pavkovic. I am an attorney from Zagreb. I am a member of the Croatian bar, and I am counsel of Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it from the nodding that counsel can understand -- not counsel, that the appellants can understand the proceedings; is that right? Okay. We have many things to accomplish today and it's going to be a long day. I'm going to make some preliminary remarks to tell you the schedule that I hope we will be able to adhere to so that everybody may be fully heard today. The purpose of today's proceedings, as you know from our order, is to hear oral argument on various aspects of Rule 115 motions to admit additional evidence. These motions were filed by the appellants Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Jospovic, Zoran Kupreskic, and Mirjan Kupreskic. In our decision dated 26 February, 2001, the Appeals Chamber addressed all of the Rule 115 motions that had been filed as of that date. That decision set out which evidence was admitted without need for further argument, which evidence was rejected without need for further argument. The Appeals Chamber decided that oral argument would be necessary on certain categories of evidence in order for the Chamber to decide whether the requirements of Rule 115 were satisfied, and that's why we are here today. But I do wish to emphasise at the outset that today's hearing is limited to those categories of evidence that were listed in the decision of 26 February, as being the subject of oral argument, and I remind the parties to restrict their submissions to those matters. In particular, the Appeals Chamber notes that since 26 February, when the decision was issued, the appellants -- some of the appellants have filed several new 115 motions. These new motions will be the subject of a separate decision, and the Appeals Chamber will not hear argument in relation to them today. In addition, the Appeals Chamber notes that there are other outstanding motions relating to material presented in other cases before this Tribunal. You are informed that a decision on these motions is being prepared. If, in light of that decision, it's necessary for appellants to file new 115 motions in relation to that material, the appellants will be advised of the time limits that will be observed with respect to that material. As is the general principle pursuant to governing documents of the Tribunal, our hearing today will be held in open session generally. Now, should it become necessary to go into closed session for reasons of protection of witnesses, then I ask counsel to raise that request at the appropriate stage when they would wish that to happen and we will rule on that. You should also know that the Appeals Chamber has already had an opportunity to view the videos that are the subject of today's proceedings, and we have done so; namely those relating to visibility conditions. It will therefore not be necessary to replay the videos in the courtroom today. A scheduling order relating to today's hearing was issued on 14 March and an order of clarification on 23 March. You are all familiar, I know, with the contents of these orders. I simply remind you that counsel for appellant Josipovic will have 45 minutes to present his oral argument. For appellants Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, they will have a combined total of 45 minutes to present their arguments. Counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic will have an hour to present his arguments. The Prosecution will have a total of one and a half hours to present its oral argument, and each group of appellants will have 10 minutes to reply. Now, it's my understanding that the Prosecution wishes to wait until all counsel for the appellants have put forward their arguments before responding, and I see Mr. Yapa nodding. We therefore have a maximum of four and a half hours of oral argument to get through today as well as questions from the bench. The proposed work schedule is as follows, but you will note as I go through it that there will be periods of 15 minutes reserved for questions from the Judges. If the Judges' questions don't take up that time, we'll move right ahead to the next appellant or the Prosecution, and hopefully that might allow us to have a 15-minute break around noontime or maybe even in the middle of the afternoon. But basically we'll go from 10.15, or whenever I finish talking, until 11.00 for Mr. Josipovic's appeal. 11.00 to 11.15 for the Judges' questions to his counsel. 11.15 to 12.00 for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. 12.00 to 12.15 for the Judges' question. If we are ahead of time at that point, we may take a 15-minute break. 12.15 to 1.15 for Vlatko Kupreskic. 1.15 to 1.30 for the Judges' questions. 1.30 to 2.30 lunch break. 2.30 to 4.00, the Prosecution. 4.00 to 4.15, Judges' questions to the Prosecution. Then the replies, 4.15 to 4.25, Mr. Josipovic. 4.25 to 4.35, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. 4.35 to 4.45, Vlatko Kupreskic. And hopefully there won't be, but if there are any outstanding matters at the end of a long day. Now, I think we'll move right into the oral argument for Mr. Josipovic who has 45 minutes. And let me just remind you that according to our decision, counsel for appellant Josipovic will present oral argument as to the following matter: Number one, why a video recording taken in Santici village on 16 April 2000 showing the lighting conditions at 5.45 a.m., or thereabouts, meets the requirements of both 115(A) that it was unavailable at the time of trial, and Rule 115(B), that the admission, its admission is required in the interests of justice. Secondly, four Croatian archive documents dated 17, 18, and 21 February 1994 and 21 March 1994. In our February decision we determined that these documents were not available at trial. Consequently, counsel is required to address the Chamber on why the interests of justice require their presentation in the record on appeal. Now, whoever is going to represent Mr. Josipovic for this purpose has the floor. It's now 10.15 until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Based on the decision of the Appeals Chamber, today we are to discuss two issues as supplemental evidence as far as the appellant Drago Josipovic is concerned. That is the first motion of Drago Josipovic which pertains to a video recording of the visibility in the village of Santici on the 16th of April 2000 in the morning hours, that is, at 5.30 a.m. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not getting anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now, Your Honour? Can you hear us?

utterances.text: Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would first like to discuss the video recording of 16th of April 2000 which was recorded in the morning at 5.30 a.m. There are two issues to be discussed here. First of all, why is it that we, the appellants, submit such a request for additional evidence. We are doing this because we believe this to be a generally-known fact, and the appellant could not have supposed that the Trial Chamber will conclude that the Witness DD from the location where she was standing would be able to identify Drago Josipovic at the distance of 35 metres. I believe that it is in the interest of justice and in the interest of truth to have the Appeals Chamber admit this evidence as the additional evidence based on the Rule 89(C). This rule says that, "The Trial Chamber can admit any relevant evidence for which it believes that has probative value." In other words, if this would assist the Trial Chamber to determine the truth based on the Rule 107 which regulates the procedure, this can also be applied before the Appeals Chamber. There is a well-established practice before this Tribunal, such as in the Tadic and Jelisic cases, that such evidence be considered as additional evidence. As far as the justice and truth is concerned, we

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: As far as the third motion of Drago Josipovic is concerned, it consists of four documents which at the request of the Defence were provided by the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I've been informed that some of the material that you are using in your oral argument deals with the content of statements of protected witnesses. What's -- what you have said in the past that falls in that category we can take care of through redaction, but I believe it would be wise, if you're going to continue to refer to the content of statements of witnesses who are protected, that we go into closed session and that would allow you to make your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not mention -- I did not refer to any protected witnesses by their names, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I used their pseudonyms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand that. But in terms of what I'm informed was closed-session testimony, I think the mere repetition of the contents -- but you can make your argument completely if we go into closed session for any portion in which you're going to discuss the contents -- in which you're going to discuss the contents. I understand you haven't identified by name the witness. Is that satisfactory to my colleagues? Yes. And the Prosecution? Okay. Why don't we go into closed session? And if you come to a point where you don't have to discuss anything that deals with closed statement -- closed -- protected witnesses, then we can go back into open session. But let me ask you already, since you're moving into the four documents, perhaps Mr. Hocking, you can inform me, is there anything that were the subject of protected witnesses or in closed session that would relate to those documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, counsel, I believe you yourself know, since this is your client's motion, whether or not there is anything in the matter that you are about to discuss which is confidential or the subject of any kind of protective order. Do you know that to be true or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will discuss a protected witness, so it would be a good idea to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Please, Registrar, put us into closed session. Okay. We are in closed session. Thank you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Now, who is going to make the argument for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since my colleague Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac and myself are, in fact, trying to argue the same facts and we believe that this is -- this has more to do with facts than with law, if you would allow us, we have divided this topic into two parts. I would be dealing with the joint issues and then my colleague would go into more specific issues. I will follow closely the decision rendered by the Appeals Chamber, and I would also have to request that the -- for the larger part, these proceedings be conducted in closed session, although the notion of the closed session is not really quite clear to me in this respect because we are quoting the testimony rendered by protected witnesses which have been made public and they -- their testimony is quoted in the public document, that is the judgement. So if we do not mention their names and we only refer to them by their pseudonyms under which they are quoted in the judgement, I don't believe that there should be any obstacle for us quoting from their statements in open session. So perhaps we could clarify this before I go on to argue my case so that I know at which point I am to request that we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You make a good point, and let me at this time point -- I might pause myself and get some advice from Mr. Hocking or the like for just what the procedure is here in terms of using closed-session testimony. You also both of you may split the argument. By my reckoning, you will have until 25 minutes after the hour, after 11.00 for both of you to complete your argument any way you split it. Let me get the advice and we'll answer your questions about closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right, I think we have an answer for you, Mr. Radovic. My counsellors tell me that these are the governing rules we should operate under: If the testimony that you are going to refer to has been the subject of public transcript, not closed-session transcript, but in transcripts that were released to the public, and a pseudonym is used, then you may refer to it in open session. However, if it was the subject of closed-session transcripts, not public transcripts, or if there is other identifying information, even though a pseudonym is used such as somebody had a husband who did this or it's easy to identify who the protected witness is by telling the circumstances surrounding them, then, again, we should go into closed session. Do those governing rules make it possible for you to go ahead? And then if you find you want to used closed session, let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first topic deals with photographs. The first issue that we have to argue relates to the videotape depicting the oath-taking ceremony of HVO units in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, I did not believe that the oath-taking ceremony was the subject of today's -- we agreed that was in the prior decision that subject to your identifying or helping us to identify exactly what frame was involved in the oath-taking that it was admitted, that it was not to be the subject of discussion today. You don't have to argue if you've just -- and I think you already have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't want to argue. I just wanted to tender the photographs and the portion of the videotape from which the stills were taken. The reason why I decided to do so was because I had sent it from Zagreb by registered mail, and I have yet to receive the confirmation from the registry that this has been received and that it is entered into the court file. I would therefore be very grateful if you could admit it now to avoid any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Let me ask -- I believe that we have received it. I believe that all the Judges have. I don't know about the Prosecution. Has the Prosecution received the identification material that our earlier decision asked that they supply?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, but to this extent, Your Honour, if I may say so, it is only a fax with the still. We have not got the photograph as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You are tendering the original now? You are tendering the original photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the original stills and the portion of the videotape with the copy of the part of the tape from which the stills were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I understand now and thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not going to argue, but this is just the technical matter, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You can begin your argument now which will take you and your co-counsel until half past 11.00. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second issue relates only to my client Zoran Kupreskic. These are -- this relates to documents specifying who was the commander of the sector which included the village of Ahmici. During the trial, two witnesses, the testimony of two witnesses was the base on which his command responsibility was determined. One of them as Abudulah Ahmic who testified what he had heard and not what he had actually seen. You can see in the court file when you actually render your appeals judgement, Abdulah Ahmic did not specify the actual time period in which Zoran Kupreskic was alleged to have command responsibility and, in the actual fact, his command responsibility involved determining who will be on guard duty in the village. The second witness, who was a protected witness -- I would therefore like to go into private session now if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Registrar, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We are reconvened and we will now hear argument from the counsel for Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic. Before you begin -- Mr. Livingston, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Mr. Abell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Abell, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I apologise. As I understand it, to make sure we are all on the same, as we say, wavelength, that according to our February decision, you will present submissions as to why the additional evidence you seek to tender on the following matters meets the requirement of 115. And those two matters fall into alibi evidence, in which you have proposed witness Marija Kupreskic and Ivica Covic and protected witnesses 1 through 8. And, two, evidence rebutting the Prosecution case about the appellants' involvement with the police. You have three proposed witnesses there and some exhibits. Now, the Appeals Chamber has already determined that the evidence falling under these two categories might meet the requirements of 115(B), namely the interests of justice. You're invited to present arguments as to primarily why it was unavailable at trial as required in 115(A). As I understand it, you are arguing four of the witnesses, AVK1, 2, 7 and 8, weren't known to you at the time. We will hear argument on that. And the remainder, you will rely upon an argument of gross negligence to demonstrate unavailability. My final remarks remind you that in accordance with our order of clarification dated 23rd of March, the submissions for today's hearing are limited to whether a prima facie case of gross negligence has been made out. That is, whether the evidence relied upon by appellant Vlatko Kupreskic taken -- if believed, taken at its highest credibility, would make out a case of gross negligence. If you succeed in that, we know that a further evidentiary hearing would need to be scheduled for the Chamber to assess the evidence and to hear any rebutting evidence. I also ask you, if you can, to let us know in advance whether you want all or portions of this to be in closed session because of what you will cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: With that, I'll let you take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May I indicate straight away that at the moment, I'm more than content to address Your Honours in open session. There will be two stages during my submissions where I would wish to go into closed session because there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You will let us know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I will indeed, when I come to it, just before I come to the most relevant part. I hope that's the most convenient way forward and will result in the maximum amount of my submissions being heard in the normal way in open session. Your Honours, I of course restrict myself to the oral argument as has just been outlined. The two groups of evidence, the alibi evidence and other matters relating to the events of the 15th of April of 1993, category A in our Rule 115 motion, and of course category C in our Rule 115 motion, evidence rebutting the Prosecution's case at trial as regards the appellant's involvement with the police. And I restrict myself to the Rule 115(A) limb, Your Honours having already ruled that the interests of justice element or limb has been made out. The argument that we advance today, and which is foreshadowed in the pleadings, on which of course we rely -- and may I say the oral argument is meant to be complementary to those pleadings - we still rely on them obviously - rather than in substitution for those pleadings, but the argument is almost exclusively based upon the contention that Vlatko Kupreskic's former lawyers, Dr. Krajina and Mr. Par, failed to exercise due diligence at Vlatko Kupreskic's trial and that they were grossly negligent in their preparation and in their presentation of the Defence on count 1, that being the persecution count, of which Vlatko Kupreskic was convicted. The contention that I've just made is based upon the assertion that there were a number of key witnesses as regards Count 1 whose evidence was, on any view, highly material to the Defence case whom his former lawyers either failed to interview at all, or if they saw them or interviewed those witnesses, failed to call them as witnesses. And, of course, the unfortunate consequence of this, which we submit is gross negligence, is that the Trial Chamber, who had to determine the issue of guilt or innocence, were deprived of the opportunity of hearing a number of manifestly important and, we submit, credible Defence witnesses whose testimony might very well have substantially changed their overall assessment of the Prosecution case against him. In our submission, the failure to call witnesses like that is grossly negligent. I would wish to say something at this stage about the applicable law. It has been conveniently set out in paragraph 16 of the decision in relation to the additional evidence under Rule 115. I'm referring, of course, to the Tadic decision which I know very well certainly one of Your Honours is, of course, very familiar with having been on the Bench that dealt with the Appeals Chamber of that matter. May I say this: Of course we accept that the burden of proving gross negligence rests upon the Defence, but this is what I ask rhetorically, and I raise it now, because it is important as to the future progress of this Rule 115 decision and, indeed, what may happen in the future. I raise this question: What of the standard of proof? The burden rests on the appellant, but what of the standard? And I'm going to, if I may, because I submit it is a fundamentally important question that will need to be resolved. I'm going, if I may, to refer Your Honours to the decision in Tadic. It's headed, "The Decision on the Appellant's Motion for the Extension of the Time Limit and the Admission of Additional Evidence." Yes, in our book of authorities, of course, and I will just refer to three or four paragraphs within that decision. Paragraph 45, in our submission, gives some guidance. "In summary, additional evidence is not admissible under Rule 115 in the absence of a reasonable explanation as to why it was not available at trial. Such an explanation must include compliance of the requirement that the moving party exercised due diligence. This conclusion is consistent with Statute and with the jurisprudence of many countries. It is not, however, dependent on that jurisdiction." Paragraph 47 deals with due diligence again. It's a necessary quality of counsel who defend accused persons. "The unavailability of additional evidence must not result from the lack of due diligence on the part of counsel who undertook the defence of the accused." And so that paragraph goes on. I needn't read every word of it. Paragraph 48 is important. "Thus due diligence is both a matter of criminal procedure regarding admissibility of evidence, and a matter of professional conduct of lawyers. In the context of the Statute and Rules, unless gross negligence is shown to exist in the conduct of either Prosecution or Defence counsel, due diligence will be presumed." That's the exception to the, as it were, availability limb of Rule 115. Paragraph 49 I rely on in this submission. "In this case, the parties agree that due diligence might have been lacking in respect of certain evidence which was not presented at trial because of a decision of the defence team to withhold it." The next sentence is crucial. "The Appeals Chamber is not, however, satisfied that there was gross professional negligence leading to a reasonable doubt as to whether a miscarriage of justice resulted. Accordingly, evidence so withheld is not admissible under Rule 115 of the Rules." A little further on in the judgement, paragraph 65, as indicated -- I'll mention paragraph 65 is cited more than once by the Prosecution in their response to this appeal but, and it's important, not the whole paragraph. The last sentence, and I'm not critical when I say this, but the last sentence of paragraph 65 of the judgement has been left out on each and every occasion that the Prosecution have cited it to Your Honours in the pleadings, and it's very important. Can I read the whole paragraph? "As indicated above," when -- and this is under the heading the material not called by Defence counsel. Paragraph 65, "As indicated above, when evidence was not called because of the advice of Defence counsel in charge at the time, it cannot be right for the Appeals Chamber to admit additional evidence in such a case even if it were to disagree with the advice given by counsel. The unity of identity between clients and counsel is indispensable to the workings of the International Tribunal. If counsel acted despite the wishes of the appellant, in the absence of protest at the time, and baring special --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel read a little bit slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, counsel, we have a request from the translating booth to go a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well, I'm sorry. I'm trying to squeeze a quart into a pint pot in terms of 60 minutes. Do forgive me. I apologise. It's just as well I've been asked to slow down because I'm coming to the crucial sentence now. "An exception applies when there is some lurking doubt that injustice may have been caused to the accused by gross professional incompetence. Such a case has not been made out by the appellant. Consequently, it cannot be said that the witnesses and material were not available to the appellant despite the exercise of due diligence." So in the decision of Tadic, the exception wasn't made out, as I understand it. The Rule 115 simply didn't get off the starting blocks. Very different case to this one. But the principle, "... an exception applies where there is some lurking doubt that injustice may have been caused to the accused by gross professional incompetence." Taken together with paragraph 49, "The Appeals Chamber is not however satisfied that there was gross professional negligence leading to a reasonable doubt as to whether a miscarriage of justice resulted." I rely on those paragraphs in the Tadic decision as providing useful guidance to Your Honours in determining what the standard of proof to be achieved by the appellants on a Rule 115 motion is. We would submit that it is clearly lower than beyond reasonable doubt or even a balance of probabilities or jurisprudence I'm sure the world over. Certainly in England, and I'm sure in -- or I surmise in America where the burden is on the Defence, it is a lower burden than when it is on the Prosecution in criminal cases. But -- and so it should be, we submit, because it is regarding the appellant not the Prosecution. But in our submission, it goes further than that. In applying the guidance upon the standard of proof to be derived from the Tadic decision, if a prima facie case of gross negligence and, of course, I agree with Your Honours's definition earlier on in the introduction of a prima facie case, of course. If a prima facie case of gross negligence on the part of Vlatko Kupreskic's former lawyers is made out on the material already submitted on paper by either side for the Appeals Chamber's consideration on the Rule 115 motion, we would submit that that would be sufficient to satisfy the standard of proof, the lurking doubt, the reasonable doubt as to whether a miscarriage of justice may have occurred. And that would render the proposed additional evidence admissible, especially so as Your Honours have already decided, on the papers, that it is in the interests of justice, subject to the gross negligence points, to hear the evidence. So if I can simply say this before I leave the law, it is our submission in those circumstances that there would in fact be no need to embark upon what would no doubt be a lengthy hearing of, in a subhearing as it were, on the issue of gross negligence, with evidence being called on either side, particularly as it would cause considerable delay and, again, I don't mean it critically when I say it, but the position appears to be from the recent pleadings, the recent urgent application by the Prosecution, urgent motion, and our recent urgent response, that despite the Rule 115 having been filed in early September - Your Honours will remember that the dates of the recent pleadings - it appears that no inquiries have been made by the Prosecution as to those matters until after the 26th of February of this year. Up until then, it appears that the Prosecution's position, presumably a considered position, was that they were content to rely upon their own written material for the entire decision to be made as to the admissibility of the proposed additional evidence under Rule 115. There has been a late change of heart by the Prosecution. We submit that there is no need to delay these proceedings, given what I've already said about the lurking doubt. We say, in other words, if we make out a prima facie case on the material either side has given, if we raise a lurking doubt, a reasonable doubt, that by gross negligence there has been -- justice has not been done, the proper evidence has not been heard, we submit that that is sufficient to make the proposed additional evidence admissible, and it will be for presumably the Trial Chamber to in due course, if need be, to assess that evidence and see where it fits into the evidence which was called on either side at trial. So that's my digression and -- forgive me, "digression" is a bad word because it's important, but that's what I would submit about the law. It is important, and that's the way that we put that. Can I now, then, turn to the argument on the material itself? Having said that in our submission all we need to achieve for admissibility is effectively to establish a prima facie case on the papers, we submit that, in fact, what there is on the papers is a formidable case of gross negligence made out against Vlatko Kupreskic's former lawyers. In other words, a substantially higher than prima facie case is made out on the papers. And may I particularly focus upon four items which -- about which frankly there can be little realistic argument by the Prosecution? And those four items, the reason I focus on those at this early stage is because each of those four items, which are documents coming from former lawyers, Dr. Krajina and Mr. Par. They are what they had to say, both at trial, at the appellate stage before they were sacked is the word we use in England -- before they were taken off the case, forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the term.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: And indeed, the letter from them to me in response to my letter to them, they speak volumes, and they speak for themselves, in our respectful submission. Putting them I hope in chronological orders, the documents are as follows: The closing address, provided at the end of the trial; the draft appellant's brief, which is at annex 2 -- that is obviously former lawyers' draft appellant's brief, annex 2. I give the reference, I don't ask Your Honours to turn it up, it's page 109 of the Rule 115 motion. Next, the draft Rule 115 motion; that's at annex 7, page 476. And finally the former lawyers' letter to me which is annex 1, at page 100, in answer to a series of questions that I posed. And may I, as it were, en passant, say this in answer to the point recently made by the Prosecution that Par and Krajina have not had a chance to respond to the allegation, it is our submission that my letter, which immediately precedes their reply, poses a series of questions which go precisely to the subject matter of the alleged gross negligence. We do, therefore have -- and they answer those questions quite fully, in our respectful submission, as they choose to do. And so we do, therefore, contrary to the Prosecution's contention, have some response to -- from them. And so we have from those four documents, a snapshot of former lawyers' thinking during the trial, at the appellant's brief stage, at their Rule 115 stage, and in response to a series of questions that I put to them. I mention very briefly, because they are in the papers before you but they are not, as it were, strictly in the Rule 115 because it's only recently happened, but you are aware from a recent motion that they were written to again, Par and Krajina, at the end of December and at the end of January, to ask them to respond further, and no further response has been received from them. Could I move on from that, please, to say this, dealing with the Defence closing brief, and I say that our pleadings speak for themselves. I'm really highlighting examples in the time allotted to me rather than going exhaustively through it, but just to give a flavour to the situation. In paragraph 121 of former lawyers' Defence closing brief, they state this: "All charges against Vlatko Kupreskic for counts 12 to 15 have been based on this testimony." And they refer to Witness Q. "And in the opinion of the Defence even for count 1" -- count 1, the persecution count, of course, "because the indictment has been set down in such a way," this is how they put it, "that should counts 12 to 15 be proven, they are to prove count 1 automatically." That was their thinking it would appear, from their own words, at the conclusion of the trial. In their letter in answer to paragraph 9 of our letter to them, querying what was meant by this particular passage, paragraph 12 of their reply, they say, "We stress that in our opinion the Prosecutor had no solid evidence against the accused Vlatko Kupreskic with respect to count 1 and that he charged him with count 1 only because he had a charge for count 2," as they call it, I think they mean 12, "which enables him in case he proved responsibility of Vlatko Kupreskic on count 2, to have it simultaneously proven that the accused participated in the persecution," i.e. qualifications from count 1. In other words, again, they are saying that a conviction on count 2 automatically means a conviction on count 1. The draft appellant's brief at page 30, the former lawyers state that "the Defence wishes to particularly point out that due to the impression" -- sorry, "the imprecision of the indictment in count 1 of the indictment in the course of the whole of the trial proceedings, the Defence was in the situation where it was unclear what exactly the subject of the accusation was, which actual committed acts is the accused charged with? Consequently the Defence was not able to respond timely with rebuttal evidence in the course of the trial. We are of the opinion that it is in the interests of justice that the Defence be allowed in the course of the appeals procedure to present all the evidence it previously considered unnecessary due to the imprecision of the indictment." There we have, in our submission, a very clear, graphic illustration of their admission that they failed to understand the scope of count 1, and they failed to realise what evidence was relevant to it or necessary for it, and they wanted to change tack, as it were, in the appeal. Paragraph 13 of their letter, I asked them about that, what is meant by the above extract that I've just read out, and really their answer in paragraph 13 - I won't read it out - but it doesn't provide, in our submission, an explanation. I hesitate to use the word "flannel," and I don't mean it offensively, but it doesn't meet the question or the explanation. And it is our submission that these passages that I've just cited, to give Your Honours a flavour, really graphically establish that the appellant's' former lawyers were unclear as to the subject matter of count 1 and were therefore unable to identify what Prosecution evidence was capable of proving count 1. Thus, they were in no position to find, to obtain or call Defence evidence in order to try to meet and/or rebut the Prosecution evidence which did in fact lay behind count 1, the allegation in count 1. Apparently their view at the trial and after the trial was that there was no case against the appellant on count 1 separate from, as they call it, count 2, and that if count 2 was dismissed, so should count 1 be, which was a clear misconception. And we submit that that position goes far beyond quoting from the Tadic case, a reasoned determination that material in question is irrelevant to the matter in hand or a litigation strategy. These were, we submit -- go far beyond. That it's not a question of tactics. It's just a question of manifestly misjudgments and errors as to the scope of the charge and as to the evidence that ought to be sought in order to deal with the charge adequately and defend it. We submit it must follow they are grossly negligent errors and it's at the root of this 115 motion that that misunderstanding, grossly negligent misunderstanding, affected the former lawyers' whole approach to the gathering of evidence on count 1 and as to what evidence was necessary and relevant to call in their then client Vlatko Kupreskic's Defence. These are, we submit, admissions that they didn't understand the charge they were defending this man on. And may I put it this way, the starting point -- as a general comment, the starting point for competent, skillful lawyers in preparing a Defence case is to be clear what the client is charged with and what the scope of that charge is. Because you need to ask the following questions when you're preparing a Defence case: What is the ambit of the charge? What do the Prosecution have to prove to make it out? What is the evidence the Prosecution are calling in support of the charge? And then how can that evidence be rebutted or explained by Defence evidence? All these, we submit, are fundamental questions that should be asked by any competent advocate, and all of those questions hang from an understanding of the scope of the charge. If one doesn't understand what the charge is, one is lost, like being in the woods without a compass. No idea which way to go, and that is a problem. We bluntly submit that to embark upon a trial such as this without a thorough grasp of what Count 1 was about is plainly grossly negligent. It's serious because it resulted in substantial material as to the alibi and as to evidence rebutting Vlatko Kupreskic's alleged involvement with the police being called. Material which is now, of course, the proposed additional evidence. It simply wasn't obtained, or if it was obtained, it simply wasn't called. Grossly negligent because it results, we submit, in really very serious consequences. Any court striving its best to do justice needs to be provided with the full picture, expects, in an adversarial system, that the Prosecution will do its duty and call all relevant, available evidence to establish their contention of guilt, and the Court is entitled to rely upon the Defence to use its best endeavors and due diligence to provide the Court with all relevant material evidence which it gathers in order to disprove the Prosecution allegation and to present the defendant's case in its best possible light. If the Defence simply fall down on providing that material to the Court, how can the Court be blamed for giving more weight to what we submit is actually rather, when one analyses it, tenuous Prosecution evidence upon which this man was convicted. They simply, the Court, did not have the full picture. They didn't have all the evidence they should have. They didn't have the opportunity to weigh that evidence and, in that sense, the Trial Chamber were deprived. It may well be that had the Trial Chamber had all the material, which we now seek to put it, it might have changed the Trial Chamber's overall assessment of the Prosecution evidence and the weight of it, and it may have changed the -- or tilted the balance in favour of the appellant Vlatko Kupreskic as to whether he was or was not guilty of Count 1. The Prosecution have argued in their pleadings that there was complaint made at the trial about the imprecision of Count 1 and that may well be so. But can I just say this: We all know, particularly here where persecution counts are tried, that they can be wide-ranging of their very nature, and the Defence should expect that. The Defence should seek clarification of the ambit of such counts from the Court as well as from the Prosecution, and if they don't get it, then the Defence should cast their net correspondingly wide. If they're going to err on one side, they should err on the side of gathering more rather than less evidence, and seeking to call as much evidence as they can in order to rebut the count that they are defending their client on. I mention, if I may, something that Your Honour mentioned during the course of oral argument this morning. We would submit that it is the duty of Defence counsel to be pessimistic rather than optimistic in discharging their duties towards their client. One can't go around defending assuming, "Oh, well, the Court's going to disbelieve that Prosecution witness, no problem. We can save a bit of time here, we won't call half the alibi evidence." The approach should be to look on -- look at the worst case scenario. Look at what the case might be if the Court is impressed by a particular witness who makes an identification. "Well, we need as much alibi evidence as we can to try and put in the scales as against what that identification witness says." So there is a duty, we submit, particularly in alibi cases which, of course, this was. The Defence have a duty to seek as many supporting alibi witnesses as possible in order to present the Defence case in its best possible light because such evidence may tip the balance in favour of the defendant in the Court's judgement. We submit that failure to call evidence of the defendant's absence from Ahmici on the 15th of April 1993, which could have been given by witnesses who were in Ahmici that day, is grossly negligent. Because it effectively left the alibi and, as Vlatko Kupreskic giving evidence in his own cause, that the person who was in the car with him when he went to Split, a person who was at Split as well, and his wife giving evidence in the cause of her husband when there were plenty of witnesses who were more independent than that who could have given a completely different strand and perspective to the alibi. They called part A which is: This is what Vlatko Kupreskic was doing on that, he went to Split and came back later. They didn't call part B which was: These are the people in Ahmici who were there and can say that Vlatko Kupreskic wasn't there at the material time. And that, we submit, would have been very important, particularly when, and I've made the point, I will make it briefly again, particularly when Mrs. Kupreskic could be said to be a -- a witness who is, perhaps, more likely to be disbelieved, more vulnerable because she's the wife of a defendant. So she needs as much support as she can. A Court is likely to be less suspicious and cynical of a wife giving evidence if she's backed up in material particulars by a number of witnesses who are much more independent. She shouldn't be left virtually on her own, as it were, to give evidence on behalf of her husband. Plus the fact that, of course, she was having a driving test on the afternoon of the 15th so there was a gap in what she said anyway. She wasn't in the region of the appellant's house at all the time so she doesn't cover the whole day. We particularly focus on the failure to call the defendant's mother, Marija Kupreskic. Of course she's also close to the defendant, but she would have been another witness. She was present all day in and around the Vlatko Kupreskic's property. In relation to her, I don't refer to it, but we rely on paragraphs 18 and 19 of our Rule 115 motion, and she does have something to add. She does have new things to add which the Court didn't hear about. She was in a position to give direct evidence not only about the appellant's absence, but the absence of any soldiers or military preparations in and around his house on the 15th, as alleged. She was in a position to deal, from her own personal knowledge, with the allegations made by certain protected witnesses, I can mention them, they are public record, L and M. She could deal with the issue of was the appellant sitting outside his shop between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m.? Did a truck arrive at dusk discharging soldiers outside the appellant's house? Were there soldiers on the balcony of the appellant's house? All these questions she could have answered. She was spoken to briefly. She was not "proofed," is what we call it in England. A statement wasn't taken from her. Ivica Civic, the brother-in-law, who was on that day looking after Vlatko Kupreskic's shop which is very near to where he lives. He was an obvious witness as well. He was also present all day. He was even mentioned in evidence at the trial by Ljubica Kupreskic as someone who was present and could help. He was never interviewed to give evidence either before or during the trial. I now want to turn to some witnesses which it would be better to deal with, if I may, in closed session, Your Honours. Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I will just say this very briefly. There can be no doubt that the CSB statements which are mentioned by AVK4 are -- did exist. There is a letter in the recent motion urgent response by us, which establishes that they exist and indeed that they did mention two other defendants. I turn now to the evidence rebutting the Prosecution case as regards Mr. Kupreskic's, Vlatko Kupreskic's, involvement with the police. I hope I can take it very briefly because of the time. The position is set out at paragraphs 61 through to 66 of the Rule 115 motion, and we submit that it is a lamentable and astonishing situation which developed in this. In their closing brief, Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic's former lawyers simply failed to refer to this police evidence at all. In their draft Rule 115 motion, they state that they proposed to adduce on appeal a statement by Miro Lazarevic who is one of the proposed additional witnesses, showing the exact period that the appellant worked for the police and the nature of his business. Kupreskic's former lawyers admit, at page 2 of this document, that they did at the time of the trial have a statement from Miro Lazarevic but that they decided not to call this witness because they considered the Prosecution evidence to be irrelevant to the case they had to meet. Well, it manifestly wasn't because that evidence was relied upon by the Trial Chamber in arriving at its guilty verdict on count 1. On page 3 of the draft Rule 115 motion, the appellant's former lawyers make a further admission, that the accused during the trial suggested that new evidence should be presented but they thought it was irrelevant and a waste of time. It was just repeating other evidence. Well, in our submission, that's clear evidence of gross negligence. It wasn't repeating other evidence. It was only supporting, and it would have supported what Vlatko Kupreskic himself had to say, again leaving the defendant as a witness in his own cause when they had in their possession independent evidence capable of supporting their own client's account. We respectfully submit that that is a lamentable situation. During his evidence, when he was being cross-examined, he specifically said that there were witnesses available who could support the evidence, and he named in his evidence Miro Lazarevic and Mohamed Trako. He actually named them, and as I've already said they had one of those statements already in their possession and I'm afraid did nothing about it. I again mention their letter to me in relation to this. "We were convinced there was no need for the additional evidence." They were seriously in error there, we submit, and the position I hope is made clear in paragraph 66. It is submitted that the appellant's former lawyers were grossly negligent in failing to identify that evidence suggestive of the appellants's involvement with the police was likely to be regarded by the Trial Chamber as significant. Further, they were grossly negligent in failing to seek to obtain and call any evidence to support the appellant's account of these documents, which were manifestly important elements in the Prosecution's case. They were failing to follow the appellant's instructions, as he told them there were these three witnesses who could help his evidence on this. Lazarevic, Trako, both of whom he named in evidence, and Ivan Cosic. That's what I say about that. May I finally in conclusion just say this? It will take me probably three or four minutes to say it. I hope I'll be allowed that indulgence, Your Honours. Vlatko Kupreskic's case should, in our respectful submission, give grave cause for concern. His former lawyers, through their own documents - remember the four documents I focused on - admit, summarising it, the following: Not understanding the nature of the charge on which their client was convicted on the scope of it; not seeing the relevance of evidence that they had, for example, the police evidence; not proofing vital alibi witnesses who would have led to a whole new strand or strut to the Defence case, which would have clearly supported and enhanced the alibi evidence already called. I want to say something now in closed session, the second and last time, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: That's just a summarising, a flavour, of the admissions effectively that they made. This we submit goes much further than litigation strategy or being selective about what evidence is called for the Defence. It is, we submit, a failure in the former lawyers' duty both to their client and to the court: A duty to their client to put his case forward in its best possible light, to look at the worst case scenario, to call all the relevant evidence, having obtained it and sought it out diligently, that could answer, rebut or explain or cast into doubt the Prosecution's evidence; and a failure of their duty to the court to make sure that the Trial Chamber had the full picture. We submit that the material we have produced and put in our Rule 115 motion and the reply and subsequent pleadings, that the Rule 115(A) limb is properly and comprehensively made out on that material. This is more, we submit, than a prima facie case, more than a lurking -- raising more than a lurking doubt that an injustice may have been done by incompetence -- and I quote there -- I cite there from that Tadic decision that I mentioned earlier. We say that by virtue of their conduct at trial, important evidence, which Your Honours have said it would be in the interests of justice to hear, was simply not placed before the Trial Chamber, evidence which may well have tilted the scales in Vlatko Kupreskic's favour. That is why we do submit in the alternative, as we said in our reply to the Prosecution's response, in the alternative to the Rule 115(A) point, that this is a case where the court's inherent jurisdiction as set out in the case of the Prosecutor against Goran Jelisic, decision on request to admit admissible evidence, 14th of December of 1999, I cite this: Considering, however, that the appeals Chamber maintains an inherent power to admit such evidence, even if it was available at trial, in cases in which its exclusion would lead to a miscarriage of justice. So we have that alternative limb that we have put in our pleadings if, and we hope that we have in our submissions, persuaded Your Honours to admit this evidence under Rule 115(A), but if not, we submit in the alternative that this is one of those cases where that Jelisic inherent jurisdiction should apply so that the evidence that should have been called in this man's trial is heard and assessed. Those are my submissions. I am very sorry. I am four minutes over time, forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but we will forgive you. Thank you very much. We will hear any questions from the judges now. I have two questions. I'll try to make them brief and that way -- I have two questions. Also before we adjourn for lunch, which should be in the vicinity of 1.00 to 2.00, one of my colleagues has very helpfully suggested that I failed earlier, this being my premier appearance as a Presiding Judge, to have the defendants themselves be identified, and so I hope before we adjourn for lunch and after I've finished the two questions, we can ask the counsel to ask their clients to identify themselves. My two questions are the following: Do you think that at the time the Kupreskic trial was being held, which is a few years ago now, that the jurisprudence in the Tribunal was developed enough or clear, so that there wasn't -- it wasn't reasonable for counsel to have some questions about exactly how a persecution charge related to more specific charges in the indictment? This is an argument which has been raised, as you know. I'd like to hear your comments on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. I fully understand that as this Tribunal has developed, jurisprudence and guidance naturally has developed. It is my submission, though, that -- and I really foreshadowed it in my submission when I said that if there is perceived imprecision in the count, then what the Defence should do is ask the Prosecution for more detail; failing that, ask the court for guidance as to more detail, so that the Defence know from the Court, the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, what evidence it is that the Prosecution rely on in relation to count 1 or what evidence the Court considers is important in relation to count 1. If there is imprecision and vagueness, the Defence have got to meet it. If the Defence don't get satisfactory answers, if I can be blunt about it, then the Defence should err on the side of safety. It is far too risky to err on the side of, "Well, we don't really know what this is about. We are going to assume that count 1 is automatically proved if count 2 is proved, and vice versa, if our client is acquitted on count 2, he'll be acquitted on count 1." That, whether there was imprecision in the indictment or not, is I'm sorry to say it, it doesn't please me to say it, but it is my professional duty to say it, that is grossly negligent. It is not looking after your client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My second and last question is: It would seem from what we know you have submitted as part of the prima facie case, that much of the new evidence which you would like to see admitted on appeal appears to be supportive of, not duplicative, I understand, but along the same lines as some other evidence submitted at trial. Now, I understand you say it was not fair to leave just the defendant with no supporting, or just the mother or just the wife or somebody. I understand your argument. But my question to you basically is: Is the nature of the submissions that you would add to, under 115 or your alternative theory, is it primarily along evidentiary lines that were probed, although you don't think at all well enough, or is there any new, for want of a better word, qualitative as opposed to quantitative evidence that you think was omitted and that these proposed witnesses and documents would put in? And if so, very briefly --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I will, I will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- refresh my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: The answer comes in two parts. I'll do the alibi second, if I may. The police evidence aspect, item C, that was quality evidence that they failed to call, for the reasons I've just explained. All -- the only evidence -- it wasn't even touched on in the closing brief. The only evidence was Vlatko Kupreskic himself left to give evidence in his own cause about the police, naming people in positions of authority who could help. He named them from the witness box. They had statements from two of them. And they failed to call -- and he named all three of them -- sorry, two in the witness box and one during the course of the trial, and they failed to call all three. That would have been a new area from people in authority. And I again, because I'm being brief, refer Your Honour to the Rule 115 motion where it sets it out in detail. So that's not just a couple of extra witnesses tagged on to a long line of witnesses, if I can put it that way. Those are important people who could have supported the defendant in a material particular, and goodness knows what effect that might have been on the Trial Chamber's view. They clearly thought that his connection with the police was a significant factor, which they clearly felt supported the correctness of the identification by L. So it goes deep into their reasoning on the conviction. How different the position might have been if they had heard those three witnesses. That's the problem. Part A, the alibi evidence, yes, some alibi evidence was called, but the alibi evidence that wasn't called is of a different type, in several ways. Firstly, the alibi evidence that wasn't called dealt with, if you like, L's alibi. He couldn't have been where he claimed to have been to identify Vlatko Kupreskic. Completely new area of evidence we seek to put in. It wasn't touched at the trial. Plus, the -- what I'll call the Ahmici strand of evidence, from the mother, from the brother-in-law, one at the house, one at the shop of Vlatko Kupreskic, all day, who could say, "We were there. He wasn't. There weren't any soldiers." I'm very helpfully reminded, and L wasn't there either. So again, these aren't just two or three new witnesses to tag on to the end of a long string all saying the same thing. These were witnesses who had something new to say who could put a different perspective on to the alibi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Thank you very much, Mr. Abell. Now, before we adjourn for lunch, which will be 1.00 to 2.00, I wonder if each of the defendants would stand and identify who he is. We can begin over here on the right. THE APPELLANT ZORAN KUPRESKIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am Zoran Kupreskic. I am the first accused in the Kupreskic and the other case, and I was convicted for the Count 2 in the indictment, although I am not guilty at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Next defendant. THE APPELLANT MIRJAN KUPRESKIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am Mirjan Kupreskic. I am Zoran Kupreskic's brother, and I would like to join my brother in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. THE APPELLANT VLATKO KUPRESKIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Vlatko Kupreskic. I am very happy with the arguments presented by my counsel here, but if the new evidence in my case are not admitted, I still believe that either I, myself, or my family will be able to prove that I have nothing to do with the events in Ahmici. THE APPELLANT DRAGO JOSIPOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Drago Josipovic. I was born in 1955. My Defence counsel is Luka Susak, as you know. As you have heard, I also feel that I deem myself to be completely innocent. THE APPELLANT SANTIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Vladimir Santic. My Defence counsel is Petar Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll now --
