utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, we will resume the appeal of Kupreskic et al. versus the Prosecutor. I believe it is the Prosecution's time, as we say, "up at bat." Who will be representing the Prosecutor for the next hour and a half?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Your Honour asked me the question as to who will be making the response. We have four members in the team. They have been tasked with responding individually in respect of submissions made by my learned friends. We will be, if Your Honour pleases, following the same order in the sense that we will be first responding to the submissions made by the counsel for Mr. Josipovic, thereafter Mr. Zoran Kupreskic and Mirjan Kupreskic and, finally, in response to the submissions made on behalf of Mr. Vlatko Kupreskic. The initial -- my task will be to make a few general observations of submissions on the matter in issue before Your Honours, and also to focus on the orders made by Your Honour by the scheduling order. In the first instance, the decision on the motion for additional evidence; secondly, the scheduling order and the order of clarification. In responding to the submissions by the learned counsel for the appellants, at the very outset I wish to emphasise that the Prosecution will endeavour to make the required submissions, keeping in mind Your Honours' decision of the 26th of February and the Scheduling Order of the 14th of March. At the same time, I wish to thank Your Honours for the order of clarification of the 23rd of March. That order, with respect, states with clarity the purpose of this hearing and focuses on the issues for the oral argument. I lay stress on the order of clarification for the reason that the counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic, I thought, made submission somewhat not quite in order or in line with the order made or the clarification made in the order of clarification. If I may refer to the order that was made, or the clarification that was made at page 4, considering that in relation to Vlatko Kupreskic, the purpose of the oral hearing is to provide an opportunity to counsel for Vlatko Kupreskic to put forward oral arguments based upon the material that it has hitherto presented to the Appeals Chamber in the 115 motion to show that where -- whether a prima facie case of gross negligence of the former counsel exists. And thereafter, there is the next step that has been initiated in Your Honours' order of the clarification, in the penultimate paragraph. "Determination of the remaining requests (B) to (E)," that is, the request made by the Prosecution, "be postponed until the Appeals Chamber has carried out an assessment as to whether the prima facie case of gross negligence is established." So to our understanding, the hearing today in respect of -- particularly in respect of Vlatko Kupreskic, is for the counsel, on the material presented by them as admitted by Your Honours' Chamber, to see whether a prima facie case of gross negligence can be made. Thereafter, Your Honours will assess the material that is presented or the arguments presented and decide on the requests made by the Prosecution. That is our understanding. Now, in the decision of the 26th of February, in respect of certain identified items of evidence, items of evidence sought to be presented by Vlatko Kupreskic, Your Honours found that the interests of justice would require the presentation of such evidence subject to the proviso that the appellant satisfied the Appeals Chamber as to the requirements of Rule 115(A). On the question of availability, that comes under Rule 115(A); the allegation of gross negligence on the part of former counsel comes into play. In the case of Drago Josipovic, the first item of evidence on which oral arguments were required was the video recording of the visibility on the 16th of April, 2000. The appellant had to present arguments on both aspects of Rule 115. As regards the second group of evidence, the appellant Josipovic was expected to satisfy the requirements of Rule 115(B). On the evidence sought to be admitted by Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, on the first category, there was a requirement for oral argument under Rule 115(B), and on the second category under both 115(A) and 115(B). The response of the Prosecution on the submissions made will be made by my colleagues in a short while. Your Honours have in the decision of the 26th of February, with respect, drawn attention to the guidelines laid down in the Tadic additional evidence decision as to the applicability of Rule 115. We have and we will try to formulate our arguments in accordance with the pronouncements in the said decision. Some parts of the reasoning in that case are peculiar to the facts of that case, but there are general principles that are relevant and material to the issues taken up in the instant case. May I be permitted to draw Your Honours' attention to a few of the salient features of that decision so far as they appear relevant and pertinent to this case? I would draw your attention, with respect, to the passage at page 14 of the judgement - it is paragraph 35 - where it is stated -- I would be reading only that passage because other passages I'll be drawing your attention only by the number but in this paragraph. Their Honours stated as follows: "As to the second requirement, it is clear from the structure of Rule 115 that interests of justice do not empower the Appeals Chamber to authorize the presentation of additional evidence if it was available to the moving party at the trial. Such an interpretation is supported by the principle of finality. Naturally, the principle of finality must be balanced against the needs to avoid a miscarriage of justice. When there could be a miscarriage, the principle of finality will not operate to prevent the admission of additional evidence that was not available at trial if that evidence would assist in the determination of guilt or innocence. It is obvious, however," this is an important passage, "that if evidence is admitted on appeal, even though it was available at trial, the principle of finality would lose much of the value which it has in any sensible system of administering justice. It is only to the extent that the Appeals Chamber is satisfied that this evidence in question was not available at trial that it would be necessary to consider whether the admission of evidence is required in the interests of justice." On this question, then, the matter of gross negligence of counsel will be relevant on the question of availability. I would also draw Your Honours' attention to certain other paragraphs in the same judgement. I will make reference only to the judgement so far as they are relevant to this presentation here. Paragraph 42, paragraph 47, 48, 49, and 50, and also, as my learned friend submitted, paragraph 65 in that same judgement. The conclusive paragraphs in that judgement, paragraphs 71 and 72, also become relevant. The question of gross negligence. The word "gross" has a sense of complete or blatant -- if I may make reference to that aspect: It is not anything that could be glossed over. The counsel presenting arguments was eloquent in criticising the former counsel. It will be our submission that the appellant has failed to show such negligence on the part of former counsel. In the Tadic decision which I referred to previously, the matter of due diligence was dealt with exhaustively and the following crucial pronouncement appeared. I'm referring to paragraph 50, which I -- which I made reference to earlier. "The Appeals Chamber considers its right to add that no counsel can be criticised for lack of due diligence in exhausting all available courses of action if that counsel makes a reasoned determination that the material in question is irrelevant to the matter in issue, even if that determination turns out to be incorrect. Counsel may have chosen not to present the evidence at trial because of his litigation strategy or because of the view taken by him of the probative value of the evidence. The determination which the Chamber has to make, except in cases where there is evidence of gross negligence, is whether the evidence was available at the time of trial, subject to that exception counsel's decision not to call evidence at trial, does not serve to make it unavailable." Before I pass on to the microphone to my colleague, mister -- Ms. Norul Rashid, I propose to deal with the aspect of due diligence. The duty to be diligent does not prescribe a standard of perfection in deciding whether counsel should have foreseen the harm and guarded against it. It has been said that the court must be cautious about the insidious subconscious influence of ex post facto knowledge. In the system that is adopted in the Tribunal, that is the adversary system, counsel has a right and a duty to decide what is technically and tactically suitable. He may decide not to call witnesses to limit or to limit cross-examination. When a case is concluded, in retrospect there may be reflection as to whether if this or that point had been taken, if certain questions had been or had not been asked, or whether if some further witness had been called, whether the result would have been different. This is hindsight. An attorney should be independent and free to act without vexation of defending allegations brought by disgruntled clients. I submit, with respect, that a lawyer is required to act in the best interests of his client, subject to an overriding duty to the court in the interests of due administration of justice. A lawyer must not be placed in a situation where he would be induced, as a matter of caution and prudence, to subordinate his independent professional judgement and proceed on a line of action which his own personal judgement would have led him to consider to be unwise. These submissions I thought I should make as a general introduction on this question of gross negligence. I would now give the floor to Ms. Norul Rashid who will make submissions on the submissions made by the counsel for Mr. Josipovic. If Your Honours have any questions? I thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, I will be responding to the oral arguments raised by learned counsel for appellant Drago Josipovic in relation to the video recording on the visibility of Ahmici taken on 16 of April 2000, and a single document which is entitled, "Massacre in the village of Ahmici was committed by this special task force of the HVO police." Your Honour, for purposes of the first portion of my submissions, we need not go into closed session, but subsequently I will be referring to the evidence of a witness who testified at closed session during the trial, and I will be making that relevant application. Your Honour, with regard to the video recording visibility, the appellant, as I understand it, Your Honour, is attempting to admit the video recording taken by his counsel in the Santici village on 16th of April 2000 in front of the house of Nazif Ahmic for the purpose of demonstrating that it was not possible to recognise a person at 5.45 a.m. due to poor visibility conditions. According to the appellant, and I'm referring to his motion, Your Honour, the proposed evidence relates to an issue raised at trial involving the identification of the appellant by Witness DD, and that would affect her credibility. Your Honour, the explanation offered by the appellant in attempting to satisfy the criteria in Rule 115(A) as to why this evidence was not available is that the Defence could not have assumed that the hearing council, that is the Trial Chamber, would have come to such a conclusion meaning that his client would be convicted. Today he added that it was a generally-known fact that the visibility conditions in Ahmici at the material time was poor. So that was an added explanation, so to speak. Your Honour, as submitted by my learned colleague earlier, at best, mere repeating that additional evidence cannot be admitted under Rule 115 in the absence of a reasonable explanation as to why it was not available at trial. In relation to the requirement of due diligence, Your Honour, it was held in the Tadic decision at paragraphs 48 to 50 that, "If counsel chose not to present the evidence at trial because of his litigation strategy or because of the probative value of the evidence, it does not make the evidence unavailable." It is submitted, Your Honour, that no reasonable explanation has been offered and that due diligence requirement has not been complied with for these reasons. The requirement of due diligence is both a matter of criminal procedure regarding the admissibility of evidence and a matter of professional conduct of lawyers according to the Appeals Chamber in Tadic. The mere assertion that the Defence was apparently certain that the Trial Chamber would not be persuaded on all available evidence to conclude that Witness DD had accurately identified the appellant at the material time does not make the evidence unavailable. The fact that the Defence made a judgement call with regard to their assessment of the credibility of Witness DD and decided that no further evidence was required to discredit her, even if that assessment turns out to be incorrect, Your Honour, that does not make the evidence unavailable according to the test in Tadic. Therefore, Your Honour, a situation where evidence is not presented as a consequence of a conscious and informed decision, that cannot amount to unavailability. In Prosecutor and Jelisic, Your Honour, that is the decision on the request to admit additional evidence dated 15 of November 2000, a similar explanation was offered by the Defence and was soundly rejected by the Appeals Chamber. The Appeals Chamber said that, "Noting that with respect to the expert's report, the Defence submits that it did not present this evidence at trial because it thought that no further insisting had been necessary." The Appeals Chamber held that, "Considering that this does not show that the evidence was unavailable at trial and, consequently, it is not necessary to consider whether the admission of this evidence would be required in the interests of justice." And lastly, Your Honour, I would respectfully agree with the Chamber's observations earlier that for counsel to forward this argument as to why evidence was not available at trial would open the floodgates. Such explanations should not be allowed, Your Honour, it would lead to, as Your Honour has observed, uncontrollable situations. That concludes my submission on Rule 115(A), Your Honour. I will now proceed to the applicability of Rule 115(B). It is my respectful submission that the interests of justice element in Rule 115(B) has not been fulfilled. The evidence is not relevant to a material issue at trial which is the credibility of Witness DD as to see in the video which has been offered by the Defence does not reflect the visibility conditions existing at the material time when Witness DD identified the appellant. And, Your Honour, further the evidence is not such that it would probably show that the conviction was unsafe as the issue of visibility was exhaustively litigated at trial. With regard to the Trial Chamber's finding in relation to Witness DD, they accepted her evidence and supported its findings for identifying two relevant criteria; namely familiarity, and opportunity. Indeed, the Trial Chamber said that the witness had known the accused as a neighbour for a great many years and had ample opportunity to identify him during the incident. Those observations are supported by Witness DD's evidence. I will just briefly highlight her evidence if we may go into closed session now, Your Honour. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the appellant's submissions earlier on Rule 89(C), the Prosecution would be grateful if Your Honour could refer to our response, our submissions in our consolidated response dated 20 of 11, 2000, where we have highlighted the distinct differences between 89(C) and Rule 115. In this case, Your Honour, this is purely a procedure under Rule 115 and that is the test the appeals Chamber must apply, and not Rule 89(C). Your Honour, in relation to the group of documents which the appellant has sought to admit, I'm gratified of course that the appellant is now of the view that the last two documents are not relevant. I take it he's withdrawing his application to admit the three documents. I will confine my submission, Your Honour, to the first -- the fourth document referred to in Your Honours' decision entitled, "The massacre in the village of Ahmici was committed by the special task force of the HVO police." Your Honour, as a matter of some preliminary observations, the Prosecution note that this document does not refer to the appellants, does not refer to any of the co-appellants, either directly or indirectly. We also note that the sources of the information contained in this document are not identified. The circumstances under which this report was prepared is not known, the purpose, the objective, are also not known. There are no indications from the appellant's counsel that he intends to adduce further evidence to explain the import of this document. The Prosecution submits, Your Honour, that the relevance of this document is limited, and that even if it was -- if it was presented at trial, it is not likely to have a bearing on the Trial Chamber's findings and final verdict. Alternatively, Your Honour, we submit that this document is either not inconsistent with the Trial Chamber's findings or are related to issues that have been fully litigated at trial. The appellant suggests that this document indicates that only the military police was involved in the attack in Ahmici, and by that extension, he is arguing that the Vitez Brigade, which -- where the appellant was a HVO reservist, was not involved at all. In relation to para 1 to 2 of the document, Your Honour, it talks about the involvement of the Jokers and a certain group of criminals released from the prison Kaonik. And then para 2 went on to talk about a HVO soldier who gave an account of what had happened in Ahmici. The issue of the military forces that were involved in the attack in Ahmici was fully litigated at trial. If I may refer Your Honour to paragraphs 128 to 135 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber considered evidence adduced by the Defence to support its case that Croatian paramilitary formations and the Jokers were responsible for much of the lawlessness rampant at the time in Vitez and its environs. In its judgement, the Trial Chamber found that a number of groups participated in the attacks, such as the military units of the HVO, members of the Jokers, and able-bodied Croatian inhabitants of Ahmici. The Prosecution -- it was the Prosecution's case all along that the perpetrators of the attack all belonged to different units of the HVO. They include the military police, the Vitezovi, the Jokers, the Black Shirts, and even the Croatian army, the HV, who was also sighted on that day. In its analysis, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber did not exactly specify which groups were involved in the entire operation in the Ahmici Santici regions and the environs. Moreover, looking at this document, Your Honour, paragraphs 4, the last -- sorry, the second last paragraph of this document, talks about this man called Darko Kraljevic. Who was the leader of this group, Vitezovi, and the Vitezovi group was also considered by the Trial Chamber in its decision. It is therefore submitted that this proposed additional evidence does not contradict, it does not show that the Trial Chamber's findings were incorrect, as the additional evidence does not demonstrate, even if accepted as correct, that it was only the Jokers and the group of prisoners that had exclusively participated in the attack. Your Honour, if I may just round out my arguments, the material issue that the document must relate to, Your Honour, is whether the appellant had participated as a reservist in the HVO. A considerable body of evidence was adduced by both Defence and the Prosecution on the status of the appellant as to whether he was an active member of the HVO, and I need not go through the evidence. They are all in the Trial Chamber's judgement. To conclude, Your Honour, the issue as to the participating forces involved in the attack in Ahmici was extensively litigated at trial. It is submitted that even if the Trial Chamber had been made aware of this document, it would not have made any different findings in relation to whether the appellant, who was a HVO reservist, had participated in the attack on 16 of April, 1993, and does not probably show that the verdict was unsafe. The video, this document, fails to meet the criteria in Rule 115 and must be rejected. That is all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Rashid. Do we have any questions for Ms. Rashid? No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RASHID
utterances.text: Grateful, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: Good afternoons, Your Honours, my name is Fabricio Guariglia. I am counsel for the Prosecution, and I will be responding to the submissions made this morning by counsel for Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. At the outset, Your Honour, I will only refer to statements from protected witnesses as reflected in the Trial Chamber's judgement, that is in the document that is already in the public domain. Therefore, I don't forecast any need to go to private session. Another point of clarification, the arguments will be presented following the categories of evidence adopted by the appeals Chamber in its 26 February, 2001 order. According to this order, there are three categories of evidence pertaining to these appellants. First one is comprised of documents relating to the command role of Zoran Kupreskic. The second one, documents relating to the identification of HVO units in the attack. And the third one are two video recordings of the visibility in Ahmici on 16 and 17 of April, 2000. And Chamber may recall that only in relation to the first two categories of evidence, there is no dispute between the parties as to their availability at trial, so the only matters that are in dispute were whether the second limb of 115 is met or not. As far as the video recordings are concerned both limbs of Rule 115 are in dispute. Another point of clarification, the Prosecution will not embark in an exercise of discussing matters pertaining to credibility and weight of evidence presented at trial, which in our submission have no place in the context of Rule 115 litigation. We will only focus on whether the evidence as presented by the appellants meets the requirements under Rule 115. The first group of evidence is first -- are documents relating to the command role of Zoran Kupreskic, and they are comprised of eight documents in total, following the Chamber's order. These are documents 6 to 13 inclusive. All documents are proffered to challenge the Trial Chamber's findings as to the command or leading role of the appellant Zoran Kupreskic, and they include a number of orders and reports either appointing or referring to sector and area commanders of the Vitez Brigade after the 16 April, 1993 attack. The appellant's position appears to be that the absence of the name of the appellant Zoran Kupreskic in all of these documents supports his contention that he was not a HVO commander and that accordingly the Trial Chamber's findings would be in error. And in particular, the appellant claims that the fact that Slavko Papic was the local commander within the Vitez Brigade of the HVO, the only unit in which the appellant could have been acting as a commander, rules out the possibility of the Trial Chamber's making a finding of any commanding position of the appellant. It is our submission that these allegations misconstrue the Trial Chamber's findings on this particular issue and the evidence supporting those findings. And that there is no inconsistency between the documents assuming the truthfulness of their contents solely for the purposes of this hearing and the Trial Chamber's conclusions as to the role of the appellant. The Trial Chamber's conclusion was that the appellant was a local HVO commander. The Trial Chamber held that contrary to the appellant's contention, his activities were not limited to assigning village guard duties. The Prosecution's theory was that Zoran Kupreskic had a leading role or a commanding role in the local HVO village guard which was in turn vertically connected to the HVO Vitez Brigade. At no point in time did the Prosecution contend that the appellant had the hierarchy of a sector or area commander, nor did the Trial Chamber affirm that he was one. In this sense, the documents are, in the Prosecution's submission, totally incapable of rendering the verdicts unsafe under Rule 115(B). Further, the Trial Chamber heard abundant evidence on the status and the role of the appellant. This evidence - and I will only highlight some of the crucial items of evidence - this evidence, including the appellant's active role in the negotiations between the HVO Santici and the Muslims in the aftermath of an incident that took place on 20 October, 1992, including his signing of a document as a representative, as a local representative of the HVO, ensuring the safety of the Muslims in the area subject to the Muslims surrendering their weapons to the HVO. The Trial Chamber also heard evidence of Nenad Santic at that time -- at that time, the Vitez company commander of the temporary home guard command, instructing third parties to deal with Zoran Kupreskic for the purposes of ensuring the safety of the returning Muslims. The Trial Chamber heard also abundant evidence pertaining to the military background of the appellant and to his inclusion in a list of reservists in the HVO Vitez Brigade and his military activities prior to the April 16, 1992 attack. And further the Trial Chamber also heard evidence pertaining to his admission to Witness JJ of his commander status and the corroborating testimonies on this last point of Witness SB, Abdulah Ahmic, Y and S, all considered in paragraphs 377 to 381 of the judgement. As to this alleged incompatibility between the appellant's status within the local HVO and Slavko Papic's role in the Vitez Brigade, more precisely within the first company of the first battalion of the Vitez Brigade, the Trial Chamber also heard abundant evidence as to the latter's active participation during the 16 April, 1993 attack, in particular, a phone call that this person, that this commander, gave to a reserve soldier, Milutin Vidovic instructing him to wake up as many Croats as possible and to warn them of the impending attack, and the Trial Chamber did not find any contradiction whatsoever between Papic's commanding position in the Vitez Brigade and the appellant's more confined status as a local HVO commander in the Ahmici area. In short, the documents proffered do not add anything that was not already before the Trial Chamber at the time of making its final decision in the case. The Prosecution submits that this evidence, if adduced at trial, could have not had any bearing on the verdict. There are two documents within this category, documents number 11 and number 12, which apparently have been proffered by the appellants to demonstrate that Zoran Kupreskic could have not been a commander. These documents are orders of the Vitez Brigade commander Mario Cerkez appointing Slavko Papic as commander of the Pirici area around the beginning of May of 1993. And the position appears to be that had the appellant Zoran Kupreskic been a commander or local HVO commander, he would have been appointed instead in this position. Now, in our submission we have said that from the -- to begin with, this is a purely speculative position, totally incapable of meeting the requirements of Rule 115(B). But in addition to that, if the position is as it appears to be, that the fact that the appellant was not appointed area commander or in another commanding position after the attack, is somehow indicative of an alleged lack of commanding status at the time of the attack, then the truth is that according to the appellant's own evidence at trial, he was, indeed, offered by Anto Bertovic, sector commander of the Vitez Brigade, the position of company commander within a sector of the defence line around July, August 1993, that is, more or less three months after the appointment of Mr. Papic. So the evidence before the Trial Chamber indicated that the appellant had a strong military background and that he was a reservist. That he had been actively involved as a representative of the local HVO, and had had a leading role in negotiations with the Muslim community during October 1992. That he had admitted to third persons that he was, indeed, a commander in the HVO. And further, that he was offered the position of company commander three or four months after the 16 April 1993 attack. It was on the basis of all this evidence considered by the Trial Chamber that the Trial Chamber made its finding in relation to the appellant's commanding role. Now, we submit that none of the documents adduced contradict or refute this evidence. It is not possible, in our submission, to conclude that had these documents been tendered at trial they would have affected the Trial Chamber's findings. It is submitted that they do not meet the requirements of Rule 115(B), and should simply not be admitted by the Appeals Chamber. I will move now to the second category of evidence, Your Honours, that is documents pertaining to the identification of the units involved in the attack. From this category, only documents 28 and 29 following the order of Your Honours' decision have survived the initial scrutiny of the Appeals Chamber. The first one, which is a document without an identifiable source, refers to a so-called Operation Spider and signals a name Pasko Ljubicic as responsible for the crimes committed in Ahmici together with an anti-terrorist platoon of the military police, the Jokers. The second document appears to be an intelligence report from the intelligence service of Herceg-Bosna, the SIS, allegedly identifying also units involved in the Ahmici massacre. Those units would be the military police including the Jokers, and the HVO Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. The position that the appellants appear to be trying to establish on the basis of these documents is that only those units and those individuals mentioned in those documents could be responsible for the crimes committed in Ahmici and that, basically, this would contradict the Trial Chamber's findings as to the appellants, both appellants', Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic's, participation in the attack. At the outset, Your Honour, the Prosecution's position is that whereas the requirement of relevance contained in the second line of Rule 115 could, if one is generous, arguably be considered to have been met by the documents, it is submitted that the evidence is definitely not such that would probably render the conviction and save as required by the same provision. At the outset, the Prosecution also submits that the Trial Chamber's judgement, far from attaching responsibility solely to local HVO members for the attack, concluded that the military operation had involved different units from the HVO including the Jokers. So already in this aspect, the documents proffered do not contradict at all the findings of the Trial Chamber. Further, the documents, on their face, and assuming are going to the truthfulness of their contents, do not exclude the participation of local HVO supporters in the attack. Here again, Your Honour, it may be pertinent to revisit briefly the evidence that the Trial Chamber had before it indicating active participation of local HVO members connected with the Vitez Brigade immediately before and during the attack, and it's important to remind that the Trial Chamber found no inconsistency between this participation and the involvement of other HVO units, notably the Jokers. Only highlighting some of the evidence before the Trial Chamber, the Trial Chamber heard evidence of a meeting organised by Nenad Santic, the local -- the HVO village guard commander around 2.00, 2.30 on 16 April in the morning on 16 April 1993 and concluded that this was the occasion in which the Croatian inhabitants of Ahmici heard about the impending attack. The Trial Chamber also heard evidence of the same Nenad Santic instructing a witness to defend a bridge during the attack. The Trial Chamber also heard evidence about the company commander of the HVO, Slavko Papic, calling Defence witness Milutin Vidovic at 4.00 a.m. on 16 April 1993 and ordering him to wake up as many Croats as possible due to the impending attack, and also had before it a certificate reflecting or certifying the wounding of a member of the HVO Vitez Brigade during the attack, that was Nikola Omasic. And finally the Trial Chamber also heard expert witness evidence from Brigadier Dzambasovic explaining in detail how the system of call-ups and messengers would act normally before a military attack started, and how that system would set in force those reservists that ought to be mobilised. So the Trial Chamber had all this evidence before it. On the basis of all this evidence, it concluded that local members of the HVO, together with other HVO units, participated actively in the attack. And in this sense, the documents adduced by the appellants do not -- do not alter at all this reconstruction of the Ahmici attack as performed by the Trial Chamber. They do not establish what they purport to establish, that the proposition that local members of the HVO participated in the attack is incompatible with the proposition that other HVO forces also participated in the attack. Finally, Your Honours, I will move to the third category of evidence, that is, the video recordings pertaining to the visibility of Ahmici on 16 and 17 April 2000. The Prosecution has dealt in extenso with these particular items of evidence in its consolidated response. The first thing is it appears at this stage to be undisputed that the evidence was undoubtedly available to counsel acting with due diligence at trial. It is submitted that the explanation offered by counsel as to why this evidence was not adduced at trial falls clearly short of constituting a showing of unavailability. The Prosecution submits that an erred prognosis of counsel cannot constitute the basis for a valid argument on unavailability of evidence. In addition, Your Honour, it is clear that the time to impeach the credibility of Witness H is over, and that the appropriate procedural stage for that particular exercise was during trial proceedings. Rule 115 is not a device to allow the parties to issue again -- to raise again issues of credibility and weight of the evidence presented at trial. In reply, appellants have resorted to the inherent authority of the Appeals Chamber to admit the evidence despite its availability at trial when the exclusion of the evidence would lead to a miscarriage of justice as affirmed by the Appeals Chamber in Tadic case. Now, no explanation is offered as to why exclusion of this particular evidence would lead to a miscarriage of justice. At this stage, the Prosecution has to submit that the exception, the miscarriage of justice exception does not, under Tadic itself, arise automatically in instances where an appellant has failed to show that the evidence was not available. I would submit that it should only be in exceptional and rare instances where this exception to the strict application or Rule 115 can be invoked. But at a minimum, with the exception to be successfully invoked, the evidence must at least satisfy the requirements of Rule 115(B), that is, it must be credible, relevant to a material issue, and such that it would probably render the conviction unsafe. Now, the evidence proffered clearly fails to meet all these requirements. It is at best only remotely relevant since it can only refer to the visibility on 16 and 17 April 2000, an issue that is immaterial for the purposes of the case. It has, if any, only negligible probative value. It has not been accompanied by any evidence or explanation as to its reliability or probative force. As a matter of fact, what the appellant is doing is they are asking you to make the following assumptions: That the visibility conditions were identical in the dawn of 16 April 1993, and 16 and 17 April 2000. And no explanation is offered as to whether this is even empirically verifiable. Further, that the visibility conditions would be identical in the house that where the appellants were identified by the witness, and the house where the videos were shot which, appellant concedes, is one of appellant's father. Here we have no information whatsoever allowing us to judge whether this is the case or not. Finally, the third assumption that you are invited to make is that all other conditions being equal, the image that is recorded by a video camera in a tape and subsequently represented by another device on the screen of a monitor is identical in precision and clarity to that captured by the human eye. It is on this basis of this purely speculative and totally unsubstantiated position that you are asked to use the exceptional remedy of the miscarriage of justice exception. Finally, Your Honour, the Prosecution notes that the appellant's reasoning conveniently overlooks central features of Witness H's testimony such as the short distance between the witness and the appellants at the time of the identification, not more than one metre, and the fact that the witness also recognised their voices. The Prosecution notes that questions pertaining to the visibility conditions not only in the witness' house but also in general, the visibility conditions in Ahmici that morning were fully litigated at trial and that counsel for the appellants vigorously cross-examined these witnesses on this issue. Further, that appellant Zoran Kupreskic, himself, testified as to this particular point. So the issue of visibility in Ahmici the day of the attack was, in our submission, fully litigated at trial. Your Honour, this concludes my submission on the motions of appellants Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic, and I apologise for the length. If Your Honours will give me leave, I will give the floor to Mr. Anthony Carmona.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Before you do that, I think it's more convenient now to ask if there are any questions that the Judges have to ask you specifically. I have one question, very short. It refers to the command, the command documents proposed in the case of Zoran. As you are aware, there's at least a good argument that can be made that he may have gotten a higher sentence because he was considered to be a "commander" of some sort. So was there any -- you tell us that there may have been a whole different level of local commanders who would not have been identified or even talked about in any of these documents which dealt with sector commanders and squad leaders and perhaps people higher up. Was there any evidence at trial that suggested that was true, that you had a kind of a local village level of hierarchy of commanders that was not part of this hierarchy that was dealt with in the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUARIGLIA
utterances.text: There was, Your Honour, and I would refer Your Honours' attention, clearly it's not -- well, it's part of the trial record to the Prosecution's closing brief where there was an extensive analysis of all of the evidence pertaining to the structure of the home guards, how these home guards have been comprised of reservists, and they were led by a local coordinator or commander that would be the point of connection between that unit and the brigade to which they would report to. This was established at trial, the vertical connection between the home guard with the Vitez Brigade and the leading position of the appellant Zoran Kupreskic in the local HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you may accede the floor to your colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am guided by the directive you have given this morning in relation to the focus and the ambit and breadth of the exercise. The gravamen of the complaint of the appellant is that there was not a just and full determination of the issues by the Trial Chamber due to the gross negligence of counsel and the unavailability of witnesses. In deference, the Prosecution submits that representation by trial counsel appearing for the appellant was adequate, and the pith and substance of the defence was adequately canvassed before the Tribunal. It is further submitted that there are multiple inherent and serious contradictions in the assertions made by the appellant and among its potential witnesses and the annexes and other documentations filed in respect of the ground re trial counsel's incompetence. In this regard, I would need to preface what I have to say with some general observations, first of which the fact that counsel may appear to have made at trial a mistaken decision, or indeed have made a decision which in retrospect has been shown to have been mistaken, is not a proper basis for finding gross negligence. It is submitted that where counsel has -- had made a decision in good faith after proper and careful consideration of the competing arguments for and against, and where appropriate, after due discussion with his client, such decision cannot be deemed incompetency. In this regard, I need to place the inevitable premise that he who moves must prove. I think in Tadic, that particular directive finds credence in paragraph 52, which I may be allowed to read, which says that a preliminary matter of general nature concerns the burden of proof. The question at issue in this motion - and this motion dealt also with the issue of incompetence - is whether the appellant is entitled to a right given to him by the appeal process which he has invoked. It is for him to establish his entitlement to the right which he claims. Accordingly, it is for the appellant to prove the elements of the entitlement. The allegations by the appellant go to the question of the diligence of his counsel at trial. In the Tadic case, the Appeals Chamber treated the question of diligence in relation to the responsibilities of trial counsel. They held that the accused has the burden of showing gross professional negligence leading to a reasonable doubt as to whether miscarriage of justice resulted. This hints at something exceptional. This finding by the Appeals Chamber was made in relation to the assessments of due diligence under Rule 115 of the rules. I will say in passing that when one looks at the factual matrix of Tadic, one would appreciate, for example, that the facts of that particular case are in fact far more prominent, far more in fact outstanding, than this present case as intimated by my learned colleague on the other side. Matter of factly, the test to be applied to determine whether or not the assistance has been effective is a twofold test. The appellant has the burden of proving gross professional negligence on the part of his counsel and that there is a reasonable doubt as to whether a miscarriage of justice has resulted. It is submitted that it should be kept in the forefront at all times that trial counsel did not have the advantage of present counsel who is now quite au courant about what evidence was relevant for the ultimate determination of guilt or innocence. The reading of the findings of the Trial Chamber is a luxury that redounds to his benefit. And in this regard, I wish to in fact in passing mention that the analysis of this Chamber proceeds upon a strong presumption, and my analysis by extension, that counsel's conduct served in the wide range of reasonable professional assistance, because the onus is on the appellant to establish the acts or omissions of the counsel alleged not to have been the result of reasonable professional judgement, and in that exercise the wisdom of hindsight has no place in the assessment process. It must be accepted that any diligent counsel must exercise a sifting process and make a selection of the evidence he considers most relevant, and in that regard is not expected to call all evidence available to him. In its decision on a motion for additional evidence in Tadic, it was said quite clinically in paragraphs 48 to 50, no counsel can be criticised for lack of due diligence in exhausting all available causes of action if that counsel makes a reasonable determination that the material in question is irrelevant to the matter in hand, even if that determination turns out to be incorrect. In fact, the standard, in other words, is one of reasonable or reasoned determination, and it is by that standard that the assessment process must have its genesis. Because it is important that when we look at a particular trial, it is important to maintain the unity of identity of client and counsel. It is a type of umbilical cord, and courts ought in fact to be loath to breach that umbilical cord unless in fact there is indeed a preponderance of evidence. In relation to the complaints, the accusation of gross negligence is also linked to the alleged failure on the part of trial counsel to comprehend the subject matter of count 1, which resulted in the failure to call relevant evidence. In its general propositions, present counsel have used former counsel's closing brief, draft grounds for appeal, former counsel's letter of response to claim gross negligence. And as I am on this whole issue of counsel's letter, I think in fact it is patently clear that when one looks at the content of counsel's letter, he was in fact constricted by not giving a full and comprehensive picture by what he saw as in fact the relationship still subsisting between in fact his former client and himself. In fact, without reference I would indicate that on three occasions there is reference to the whole question of client-attorney privilege. It is passing strange that the two letters referred to my friend subsequently, which in fact is not before this Tribunal, that there is absolutely nothing mentioned about a waiver of privilege, notwithstanding Article 8(2)(b) of in fact the code of conduct that obtains in this jurisdiction in relation to the whole question of confidentiality and counsel-client privilege. Trial counsel was of the opinion, it is the submission of the appellant, that if the Prosecution was able to prove the charges on count 12 to 15, their client would automatically also be found guilty of count 1. As a result of this view, trial counsel did not call the right evidence to rebut the Prosecution case on count 1. This is the contention. The appellant finds support, as I said before, in the documents I've mentioned before. Now, even if trial counsel assumed that Prosecution evidence of counts 12 to 15 would also cover the charges in count 1, the trial record shows no indication that trial counsel was grossly negligent in the defence of charges in count 1. The record does not reveal that trial counsel were in no position to seek --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down, especially when reading?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Could you slow down for the translator?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Certainly. I'm accordingly guided, Your Honour. The record does not reveal that trial counsel were in no position to seek and obtain and call evidence to meet and rebut the Prosecution's evidence behind the allegations that are in count 1. It is the submission of the Prosecution that trial counsel made every effort to identify the charges in count 1 that needed to be rebutted. The Defence closing brief, which summarises the Defence case presented at trial, reveals that as well. In that document, trial counsel identifies all possible charges that could fall under count 1, critically examining the evidence led by the Prosecution in its attempts to corroborate those charges and put forward arguments in rebuttal of this evidence. A great majority of the Defence closing brief is devoted to this exercise in relation to count 1, and has touched on practically all the issues that were considered relevant by the Trial Chamber re count 1. An analysis of that closing brief and the Trial Chamber's legal findings as to Vlatko Kupreskic's guilt under count 1 again illustrates that trial counsel had presented a proper defence. And in that regard I wish to refer to the consolidated response motion of the Prosecution outlining those paragraphs. The vagueness and imprecision in the indictment with respect to count 1 was subject to complaints by all Defence counsel at trial. Trial counsel of Vlatko Kupreskic was not the only counsel that complained about an alleged immateriality in the proceedings. All six accused filed motions vis-a-vis the form of the indictment in which they argued the lack of specificity on the indictment. The Prosecution submits that the correspondence between trial and present counsel adds little to what was already known and discussed at trial. This could not possibly indicate negligence. It is passing strange that there are no such claims in relation to the other attorneys who in fact appeared at trial. The third document submitted by the appellant is the draft appeals motion of trial counsel and brief. A brief in draft form has little probative value. It will be highly unfair if the Appeals Chamber would find that trial counsel acted with gross negligence on the basis of views expressed in a draft document. For this reason alone, this document cannot be relied upon as a demonstration of gross negligence of trial counsel at trial. I dare say finally on this point, it is misconceived to apportion blame to trial counsel on the basis of a draft document as it is misconceived to rely on a draft document of a Trial Chamber judge found in the hallway. In relation to the whole issue of additional evidence, counsel has focused on alibi evidence and other matters relating to the 15th of April and evidence rebutting the Prosecution's case as regards the appellant's involvement with the police. It is important to note what is required in the context of an alibi defence. An alibi can be disproved or rebutted. It is expected that trial counsel would take all reasonable steps to secure witnesses, and this could require the calling of either affirmative or negative evidence, affirmative in the form of evidence that positively evinces that the accused was in a different place at a given time, or in the latter, evidence that is led to the effect, "I don't know where he was but he was not at the locus in quo." The first type of evidence is stronger by its very nature and possesses greater cogency and reliability. The latter does not. Leading evidence of the absence of an accused will depend on so many variable subjective factors. It is submitted that when one looks at the evidence led by trial counsel, the evidence in support of alibi, entailed leading evidence tending to show that by reason of the presence of the defendant at a particular place, on a particular area, or at a particular time, he was not or was not unlikely to have been at the place where the offence is alleged to have been committed at the time of the alleged commission. In toto sequitur, evidence which merely indicates that the defendant was not present at the scene of the crime, with no positive assertion as to where he was, is not evidence in support of an alibi, and it is the submission of the state that if one looks at the evidence of the various witnesses, it does not have the type of substantive quality as the evidence that trial counsel led. Let us examine these witnesses. We refer to additional evidence involving Marija Kupreskic, Ivica Covic, AVK1, 2, 3, 4, 7, and 8. In terms of there are two types of evidence, evidence unavailable --

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise for interrupting my learned friend. I'm just a little concerned if we are going to mention protected witnesses, would it not be wiser to go into closed session? I do apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: I'm grateful to my friend. I do apologise. I was in full flight and in those circumstances I do in fact make the application for a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: All right. But you will let us know when you're done with closed session because indeed there is a tendency to keep going until -- all right. We will go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARMONA
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you for your intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: We now come to the last and briefest portion of our appeal and we will have ten minutes rebuttal by the three Defence counsel beginning with Mr. Susak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would first of all like to refer to Rule 89(C) which has been erroneously interpreted by the Prosecution because this Rule stipulates that a Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. Therefore, the claim proffered by the Prosecution that I have misinterpreted this rule is not correct. According to Rule 107 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence regulating the procedure before the trial -- indicates that the same procedure will be applied to appeal proceedings. We believe that the videotape and the massacre in Ahmici, that they both fulfil the condition required for them to be introduced into evidence. Madam Prosecutor likewise erroneously indicated that there was enough evidence to identify Drago Josipovic by Witness DD stating that it was possible for him to -- that witness to identify Mr. Josipovic. She probably misunderstood me because I -- what I was talking about was whether it was possible for the witness to identify Drago Josipovic from the house where she was standing; that is, in front of Asim Ahmic's house. The reason why this piece of information is important for me is to be able to determine whether Witness DD spoke the truth or not. Also relating to this issue, I have to state right at the outset that the Appeals Chamber, in its decision, accepted the statement of Witness CA who was a Court witness and it is precisely the statement of this witness that impeaches the credibility of Witness DD. The Appeals Chamber has accepted this statement without prejudice as specified in the decision. Madam Prosecutor likewise said that I stated that Drago Josipovic would not be convicted, would not be considered guilty; that is not correct. What I said was that the testimony of Witness DD was not true and that it could not be taken into account as such. The judgement rendered by the Trial Chamber came as a great surprise to me and so did the explanations provided by the Madam Prosecutor here today. Witness DD remains to be controversial and the Trial Chamber did not approach this issue in the same manner as it did other related issues in the same case. Witness DD gave her statement to the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor five years after the event. It is therefore untrue when the Prosecutor states that the -- that Witness DD speaks the truth because she was his neighbour and she knew him well. The statement was taken, by an investigator, from this witness once the indictment had been not only amended but was already made public and confirmed by the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: It is my belief that the Appeals Chamber can accept the additional evidence in order to avoid any miscarriage of justice. And it is also my belief that this piece of evidence, this videotape, should also be admitted as additional evidence just as the document "Massacre in Ahmici," and the Appeals Chamber has already indicated in its decision the importance of this document in the proceedings which is quite contrary to what Madam Prosecutor has been saying. In the Kordic judgement, it is indicated that the soldiers or, rather, military police officers attacked the village of Ahmici and that the group, which was under the command of Witness AT, attacked Muzafer Puscul's house yet, according to the judgement, it was mentioned that these were members of the local police force. After all, this document also indicates that it would follow from this document that the village was attacked by members of the military police and also by Jokers who were also part of the operation. I propose that both these elements be admitted as additional evidence in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Judges, do you have any questions? No? Okay, thank you Mr. Susak. Go ahead, Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am quite used to a legal system in which the actual correct determination of the facts is very important, a search for material facts for the truth in which a judgement is as close as possible to the actual state of affairs. I believe that this Court pursues the same end because unless we establish the facts correctly, we cannot make legal decisions. But when I listen to what the Prosecution has been saying about us, I have been quite amazed. And the question that I ask myself is whether the Prosecution cares about the actual truth or not. The first objection proffered by the Prosecution refers to documents relating to Zoran Kupreskic as a local commander. Local commander, Zoran Kupreskic was a local commander until such time when we -- when he ceased to be the local commander which was in late January or early February. On the 22nd of October 1992, he was the coordinator for village guards, and everything he did after the 22nd of October, the only thing he did was to ensure that the Muslim neighbours were able to return to the village and to make sure that the coexistence of Croats and Muslims in Ahmici should continue just as it went on for such a long time, and actually it existed until some persons from -- came from the outside and did all this that actually happened there. Since all the documents that are in existence speak about persons who were in charge, who were commanders, and since the Prosecutor does not have a single document indicating that Zoran Kupreskic was a commander, we now have a situation in which we say, yes, somebody called Milutin then somebody else called Slavko Papic, not Zarko Papic but Slavko Papic called Milutin, but there is also a meeting attended by Dragan Vidovic in the early morning of the 15th of April. But if Zoran Kupreskic was any kind of a local commander, would not -- would it not be logical for him to be invited either to the meeting or to notify him that he is to carry out any operations. No, this is just glossed over, "... but Zarko called this guy and Pero called that guy." This will not make it possible for us to determine facts. Then a counter-argument proffered by the Prosecution is that four months later, the battalion commander asked Zoran Kupreskic whether he would like to be a company commander, and a great deal of authority is then imputed to Zoran Kupreskic. It is a well-known, undisputed fact that Zoran Kupreskic graduated from the school of reserve officers in the former Yugoslavia. There was no professional or reserve officers in the army of Bosnian Croats at that time, and it was quite natural at that time that when somebody saw that it was in his file that he was a reserve officer, to offer him such a job. The reason why I have to hurry up is because my time is limited. There is a document indicating that later on when he was proposed to be commissioned as an officer, it was specified that he was not in favour of the HDZ policy, and that he was not in favour of any policies aimed at dividing the population on ethnic grounds. Therefore, Your Honours, we would like you to bear in mind who it was who was called in the village of Ahmici, that it was not Zoran Kupreskic. He would have been called if he was -- if he had been a local commander, and all the relevant documents indicate that he did not have a place in the chain of command. The trouble that we have in this case is Dayton indicating that the Prosecutors never served in the army or they do not have a notion -- they do not know what national service is and what an army is -- what is the organisation of the armed forces in those countries which do have national service, and that is why we have had to prove to them that a reserve -- member of the reserve forces is a civilian until such time as he is mobilised. And now we have a term -- we ended up having this term active reserve officer which is ridiculous. We called brigadier of the Muslim army who was in -- also in the federation army, Asim Dzambasovic. He explained everything. We were very happy with his testimony. He explained everything, how one becomes a member of the reserve force, when one becomes an active service personnel. But in the judgement, there is nothing about his testimony. Although he was a Prosecution witness, it turns out that his testimony was more in favour of the Defence than of the Prosecution. He also explained the way in which special purposes units carry out their actions, the kind of weapons that they had, those special units, how one ensures that certain actions are kept secret if you want to get the element of surprise. But the judgement does not take any account of this. It would turn out that we questioned Asim Dzambasovic for no reason, it was completely pointless the whole testimony and questioning. The next issue that the Prosecution has something to say is the issue of the home guard. Unfortunately, all the documents relating to the home guard have been rejected. And now, willy-nilly, I have to give a little explanation in this respect. In the Vitez area, as one of the documents that have been rejected indicates, there are persons who have been -- who were part of the command of the home guard although it is quite clear that the home guard was never set up properly, because all the reserve officers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Counsel, will you slow down a bit because the translators just can't pick up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just trying to save us some time. Precisely because of this circumstance, we wanted to have these documents relating to the home guard accepted because we wanted to determine the actual situation. All the documents that we were able to obtain were also available to the Prosecution. None of the documents from the archives that we used were not unavailable to Prosecution. It also refers to the documents from the president of the republic because all the documents were given both to us and to them. When the Prosecutor talks about who participated in the attack on Ahmici, they enumerate various units but they forget the judgement that was rendered in public in the Kordic/Cerkez case where the Trial Chamber stated that the commander of the Vitez Brigade is acquitted of charges relating to his brigade taking part in the attack. The Prosecution should have made a note that a different determination of fact was made in another case. As an argument in favour of the thesis that the locals also took part in the Ahmici attack, they mentioned this of Nikola Omazic and the actual fact of his wounding. When this happened to this person, he was a civilian. Let us not forget that in every armed conflict between two armed forces or even, if you like, when you have an exchange of gunfire or even when only one side is opening fire, there is always the possibility of civilian casualties, bullets can go astray. And finally, the videotapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: One minute on the videotapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take some time from my colleague, the ten minutes that have been allotted to her, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. It was very clear from the scheduling order that the ten minutes was to incorporate both of you. It's up to the both of you to decide who took the ten minutes, and I think you've taken the ten minutes. So I'm back to square one. You have one minute to talk about the video and then -- otherwise it's not fair to the other counsel. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I will use my minute as follows: The 16th of April is in a few days. If the Prosecutor brings into question the visibility on the 16th of April, they can send an investigator to Ahmici on the 16th of April and they can tape the visibility as it is on the 16th of April. Do I -- I'm still within my time limit. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I don't have a watch with a second hand on it, but I think, at most, you've got 20 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The actual taping was done by a professional cameraman who does work for TV. We were present when it was taped and it was done at the proposal of Zoran Kupreskic because we did not have any other idea how we could impeach Witness H. If I can have just one more minute, you allowed this to my colleague, to my English colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm afraid not. I think we have to adhere to our rules. I think we have fully your argument from your main argument, from your rebuttal, and from your papers. So I'll thank you, and unless the Judges have any questions for you, we'll go on to Mr. Abell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. Can I deal first of all with the submissions on the evidence advanced by my learned friend, Mr. Carmona, this afternoon. Can I put it in this way: What it comes to is that those submissions made this afternoon are basically, and I say this with all due respect, a summary of the Prosecution's consolidated response which was filed some time ago. We rely, still, upon our Rule 115 reply dated the 15th of December of last year, which we submit comprehensively deals with all the points advanced in that response by the Prosecution and comprehensively therefore deals with the points advanced today by my learned friend. But I will, if I may, just briefly, I hope briefly in the time allowed to me, deal with some of the points he made. Firstly, I hope not confusingly, may I take it in reverse order. The police evidence, I think I can deal with that really quite swiftly. We put it in this way, Your Honours: Not calling the supporting evidence from independent sources is being suggested by the Prosecution in this Court to be a considered, and I use his words "... and informed litigation strategy," or stance and, therefore, was not grossly negligent. We, with respect, to the Prosecution, profoundly disagree with the Prosecution's submission for the following reasons: Firstly, the evidence as to police involvement was clearly regarded by the Trial Chamber as significant evidence and as evidence which assisted them in reaching their guilty verdict on Count 1. It tied in and supported, in their view, the identification evidence taken with the other, as we submit, rather tenuous strands of evidence against Vlatko Kupreskic in this case. Secondly, the evidence as to police involvement apparently was adduced by the Prosecution at trial without objection, so presumably it must have been conceded at trial that it was relevant to some issue. One would have expected therefore the Defence would be on notice, if it's relevant to an issue, that whatever the issue was they ought to find out what it was and also they ought to call evidence to rebut or explain or neutralise that issue. Thirdly, the client, Vlatko Kupreskic, a layman, in the witness box named two of the three proposed witnesses we wish to call as additional evidence. Former lawyers had a statement from one of those witnesses and were on notice of the names of the others, and yet they advised their client not to call the evidence because they considered it was irrelevant, and a factual error, which I know it's very easy to fall into, but it's not right to say that Ljubica Kupreskic gave evidence in support of her husband about these documents. Vlatko Kupreskic stood alone. The only evidence we can find in her evidence is transcript page 9396, lines 19 to 25, where Mr. Terrier in cross-examining Ljubica Kupreskic, that's the defendant's wife -- I'm sorry, making -- forgive me, making submissions, I'm helpfully corrected by my learned co-counsel, mentions the document but says he wasn't proposing to ask Mrs. Kupreskic about it because, I quote, "I don't think she would know that, whether she knew anything special," et cetera. It seems to be conceded at trial by the Prosecution, but it's not a document the lady could speak to. The only person called who could speak to the document was the now appellant Vlatko Kupreskic. We submit quite bluntly that it is about the clearest case of gross professional negligence that one could see, quite frankly, and I hope I'm not quite putting it too high. It certainly is well above a prima facie case. Can I turn to the alibi evidence just briefly and remind Your Honours that, of course, under that category is other evidence relating to the 15th of April, 1993, which includes, for instance, the presence of soldiers in or around the Vlatko Kupreskic home. The alibi evidence which was failed to be called, was not called by former lawyers, was relevant. This court, Your Honours, have decided that it goes to an issue in the case, and indeed would be subject to the gross negligence point, in the interests of justice, to hear. We are obviously concerned about it. It falls into two different strands. It's not right to say that it's not just some more evidence that would, as it were, stand in a long line of alibi witnesses. The strand that was called was the evidence that Vlatko Kupreskic went to Split. What wasn't called is the evidence to show that Witness L was not where he claimed he would have been to identify Vlatko Kupreskic, independent evidence of Kupreskic being in Split, but because it's independent, highly capable of being supportive of the correctness of Kupreskic's alibi as being in Split. Secondly, the second strand of evidence was that Vlatko Kupreskic was not in Ahmici during the course of the day - this is the evidence that wasn't called - nor were soldiers in or around or near his house on the afternoon of the 15th -- again, an independent strand of evidence but capable of supporting the other two strands of evidence. One strand was called. Three strands of alibi evidence should have been called. We reject with respect the Prosecution's submission that the strand of evidence to say Kupreskic wasn't in Ahmici is not alibi evidence. It is. If we -- if evidence is called to say he's not where the Prosecution say he would have been, that means he must be elsewhere. It's evidence in support as an alibi. He's not in the place the Prosecution says he is. So all that evidence is capable of cumulatively - and evidence like this has to be seen cumulatively - supporting the evidence that was called and of enhancing it. I just briefly would wish to go into closed session to just deal very, very briefly with some protected witnesses. I'm conscious of the fact that I'm running out of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You've got, I would estimate, two minutes, and you may go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Very well. Might I just in two sentences -- I really don't want to be unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The two sentences begin now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Yes. The point about the standard of proof and the order of clarification, we do submit -- stand by the submissions I made this morning, that the standard of proof is a low one, a lurking doubt, or a prima facie case of professional -- gross professional negligence, and that if that is made out to that standard, there really is no need for there to be a lengthy hearing involving evidence called live by both sides. We submit the four documents in particular we have referred to, made by Par and Krajina at the times I have mentioned, really do speak for themselves, and the inferences can be drawn. A mighty long sentence the second one. Sorry for that. I'll now sit down while my credit remains good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do we have any questions for Mr. Abell?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Go ahead. We are going to conclude. I have just a few brief remarks to tell you of how we project the future of this appeal so you can be aware. The Appeals Chamber plans to issue as prompt a decision on the matters that we have discussed today as is feasible. We are aware, as I mentioned earlier, there are some other pending motions, and those decisions will likewise be issued as promptly as it is possible for us to issue them. At the same time that we issue our decision, we contemplate issuing, simultaneously or immediately following, a briefing schedule for the actual appeals briefs. We hope that enough decisions on the 115 business and allied concerns will have been issued by then so that you will be able to make use of that. Now, I am also aware that there may be other 115 issues coming up. I hope not, but one has been alluded to today, which we haven't even received yet, so one can't be sure, but I believe it will be our practice to go ahead and adhere to the scheduling order for the main briefs. Either the subsequent decisions will be issued in time for the preparation of the brief or it may be that you'll be allowed to file a short, supplementary brief if it won't. Our strongest desire is to see the oral argument in this appeal -- meaning the briefs will have been filed by the end of June so that we can have a judgement in the fall before some of us depart from the scene. I'm sure you don't want to begin the process all over again. So we will depend upon the goodwill and the expeditious efforts of counsel and will proceed as fast as we can, commensurate with the rights of everybody involved. The last thing I want to mention is that the rule requirement of a Status Conference every 120 days means that we will schedule one for the 10th of April at 4.00, but you'll get a separate written notice of that. I think that concludes all the business we have to take up today. Thank you all for your diligence. Mr. Abell?

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: Could we, out of courtesy -- as you mentioned, will there be any 115 motions? We should tell you we do anticipate -- it won't be very big. There will be one very soon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I did not say there was a ban on them. I evidenced a hope that we wouldn't see too many of them. We will do our best with them, but I hope you will use discretion and reserve in bringing other ones and they will not, to the best of our ability, hold up going ahead with the briefing schedule so that we can take care of this appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ABELL
utterances.text: We understand that. If I may say so, it echoes what my lay client Mr. Kupreskic said when he was asked to identify himself, that things are changing in the Ahmici area and evidence appears to be coming out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. Thank you, counsel, and thank you to all the other people, and have a good weekend. Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Your Honour. You have just mentioned that we will have an opportunity to write a supplement to the brief. Does that also apply to the motions that we have submitted before you decide on the submissions that were already made, based on Rule 115?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, no. Let me just clarify that. After you get a decision on the matters discussed today -- anything that was involved in today's appeal, when you get that decision, hopefully by that time it will be possible to give you decisions on some without going into details of the other pending motions. So hopefully you will have decisions on many of these at the time that a briefing schedule begins. In the event that we are not able to issue every decision at the same time we issue the decision on all the matters discussed today, and any others that we can do, we will go ahead with the briefing schedule. In the event, then, that a decision has to come down after the briefing schedule has begun on a subsequent 115 motion, we will at least entertain the possibility of letting you file a supplementary brief, if it's so far along in the briefing process that it wouldn't be fair for you not to. But we are not asking you to file any briefs before the decisions come down in today's issues. Okay? Again, have a nice weekend.
